title: The Annunciation (25 March)
hookLine: nine months before Christmas; once the start of the new year in England

lines: ONCE, THE TURN OF THE YEAR.
cards: Count forward nine months from today and you land on Christmas. The feast of the angel's visit to Mary is kept in spring, a pregnancy's length before the birth.
And for a long stretch of English history, this was also the day the year itself turned over. Not midwinter. Late March.
Dates on letters and legal papers changed their year here, on the feast English people called Lady Day. A country turned its calendar on a conversation in Nazareth. Today, the Annunciation.

teach.b: Luke opens the scene with a time stamp of his own: "And in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth." The sixth month of her cousin Elizabeth's pregnancy.
The story itself is already counting months.

teach.h: HAIL, THE LORD IS WITH THEE.
teach.b: Gabriel greets her: "Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Luke says she was troubled, and wondered what kind of greeting this was.
Then the message: she will conceive and bear a son, and call his name Jesus. She asks how, since she has no husband.

teach.h: BE IT UNTO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.
teach.b: The angel answers, and she replies: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." Advent already stayed with that yes. Today the feast asks something else of it: when.
Christian tradition holds that this is the moment God took flesh, not at the manger but here, hidden, months before anyone could see.
Some readers see that thinking behind keeping the feast nine months before Christmas, and behind once starting the year here. The new thing had begun, even if it didn't show.
For a long time, church bells marked the moment every day too.

teach.h: THE ANGELUS: A BELL AT NOON.
teach.b: The Angelus, rung in some Catholic and Anglican places morning, noon and evening, is a short prayer that walks back through this scene: the angel's message, Mary's answer, and the Word made flesh.
Tradition pictures farmers stopping in the fields at the bell, noon in the middle of a working day, set aside to remember Mary's yes.

how: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches keep the Annunciation as a major feast in spring, and in some places the Angelus is still rung or prayed at morning, noon and evening.

games.q: you're Mary. an angel has just greeted you as highly favoured and told you you'll bear a son. you have no husband. what do you say first?
o: say nothing and wait for the angel to leave.
games.why: she asks how, since she has no husband. the angel answers, and then she says, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word."

practice: Practice a noon pause now, so it's ready when midday comes: stop your hands, look up, and take three slow breaths.
If you pray, say Mary's answer, be it unto me according to thy word; if you don't, ask yourself what you're saying yes to today, and sit in the quiet that follows.

wordCard.voice: The Annunciation. The angel's announcement to Mary, kept as a feast nine months before Christmas, the hidden start of the Christmas story.
